qs.q: A young adult under 40 years old presents with erythema nodosum, peripheral arthropathy, uveitis, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of this multisystem disorder?
o: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to occupational organic dusts
Autoantibody production against type IV collagen in the membrane
Direct bacterial infection of the alveolar walls by tuberculosis
Abnormal CD4 mediated cell reaction to an unknown antigen
qs.e: Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-caseating granulomatous inflammation driven by an abnormal CD4-mediated cell reaction to an unknown antigen. It is not caused by active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection despite forming granulomas.

qs.q: A 32-year-old man presents with erythema nodosum, peripheral arthropathy, uveitis, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations reveal hypercalcemia. Which of the following is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism for the hypercalcemia in this multisystem granulomatous disorder?
o: Excessive dietary calcium absorption via altered gut mucosa
Increased formation of calcitriol by alveolar macrophages
Autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid gland receptors
Direct destruction of bony trabeculae by systemic granulomas
qs.e: Hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis occurs due to increased formation of calcitriol by the alveolar macrophages. It is not caused by direct bone destruction or parathyroid receptor autoimmunity.

qs.q: A 38-year-old man with sarcoidosis presents with severe uveitis and pulmonary impairment requiring systemic intervention. Which medication is specifically indicated to commence treatment for these manifestations?
qs.e: Prednisolone (20-40 mg/day) is commenced if pulmonary impairment, hypercalcemia, renal impairment, or uveitis are present. Azithromycin and diethylcarbamazine are not the primary systemic agents for sarcoidosis systemic management.

ai.title: Uveitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Uveitis is inflammation of the uveal tract that can be anterior, intermediate, posterior or panuveitis. In low‑resource settings the most common causes are infections (TB, HIV, malaria, schistosomiasis) and autoimmune diseases (spondyloarthritis, sarcoidosis). Rapid recognition and treatment prevent blindness.

sections.p: Uveitis refers to inflammation of the iris, ciliary body, choroid or retina. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history, visual acuity, intra‑ocular pressure, slit‑lamp or indirect ophthalmoscopy. In resource‑poor settings a simple eye‑exam with a pen‑light and a hand‑held ophthalmoscope can identify the key features.
b: Anterior uveitis – pain, redness, photophobia, blurred vision, ciliary flush, keratic precipitates
Intermediate uveitis – floaters, blurred vision, mild pain, cells in vitreous
Posterior uveitis – painless vision loss, floaters, chorioretinal lesions

t.b: Measures functional loss – a drop of 2 lines suggests significant inflammation
Elevated IOP indicates steroid‑induced pressure or angle‑closure risk
Detects cells, flare, keratic precipitates, synechiae

sections.p: The SUN (Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature) grading system is used worldwide. It grades anterior chamber cells and flare, vitreous haze and retinal lesions. In low‑resource settings, a simplified grading (0–4) based on visible cells and symptoms is practical.

t.b: Assesses severity and guides treatment intensity

sections.p: In East Africa and similar settings the top causes are infectious. Autoimmune causes are less common but still important.
b: • Herpes zoster ophthalmicus – anterior uveitis with dermatomal rash

sections.p: Patients report eye pain, redness, photophobia, blurred or painless vision loss, floaters or flashes. Systemic symptoms may accompany infectious or autoimmune causes.
b: Panuveitis – combination of above, often severe

sections.p: Investigations are tailored to available resources. Start with basic tests; if unavailable, rely on clinical judgment and empirical treatment.

t.b: Positive indicates need for opportunistic infection workup and possible steroid avoidance
Positive requires penicillin therapy; untreated can cause irreversible blindness
Hilar lymphadenopathy suggests sarcoidosis or TB; guides further TB workup

sections.p: Urgent red flags include sudden severe vision loss, pain with eye movement, hypopyon, or signs of angle‑closure. Complications can be sight‑threatening or systemic.

Treat the underlying cause first. Steroids are the mainstay for non‑infectious uveitis; infectious uveitis requires specific antimicrobial therapy. Supportive care includes cycloplegics, IOP control and monitoring.
b: • Daily visual acuity and IOP in first week
• Repeat slit‑lamp every 3–5 days until stable

sections.p: Regular follow‑up is essential to detect recurrences and complications. Prevention focuses on treating systemic diseases and avoiding known triggers.
b: Patient education – avoid eye trauma, use protective eyewear

sections.p: Several conditions mimic uveitis; distinguishing features are key.
b: Scleritis – deep, boring pain, scleral redness, no AC cells

sections.p: Some tests may be falsely normal or abnormal in low‑resource settings.
b: Chest X‑ray – small nodules may be missed; consider CT if available

faq.q: What is the most common type of uveitis in East Africa?
faq.a: Anterior uveitis, often linked to spondyloarthritis or infectious triggers like TB.
Yes, malaria can lead to retinal haemorrhages and optic disc swelling, presenting as posterior uveitis.

faq.q: When should I start systemic steroids?
faq.a: When inflammation is severe, posterior or panuveitis, or if vision is threatened; only after ruling out active infection.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with unilateral eye pain, redness and photophobia. What is the first test you order? — Check for anterior chamber cells and flare; order a rapid HIV test and syphilis RPR to rule out infectious causes.
A patient with known TB develops eye pain and blurred vision. What is the safest initial treatment? — Start anti‑TB therapy; avoid systemic steroids until TB is controlled.
A child has painless vision loss and a hypopyon. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Posterior uveitis; obtain a chest X‑ray for TB and start empiric anti‑TB therapy.
You suspect acute anterior uveitis in a patient with ankylosing spondylitis. What drug should you avoid? — Long‑term systemic steroids; use topical steroids instead.
During ward rounds you notice a patient with eye pain and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the red flag? — Angle‑closure glaucoma; urgent IOP lowering and referral.
A patient with chronic uveitis has developed a cataract. What is the most common cause? — Long‑term steroid use.
You have a patient with eye pain, photophobia, and a history of recent malaria treatment. What is a possible drug‑induced cause? — Antimalarial (chloroquine) toxicity causing retinal damage.
